newsitem.title: USA: Emerging markets seen still strong in 2H - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Emerging markets seen still strong in 2H - analyst.

text.p: Emerging markets should keep up their strong performance in the second half of 1997, an HSBC James Capel strategist said Tuesday.
Geoffrey Dennis, global emerging markets strategist, wrote in a report that 1997 could be the best year in the emerging markets since 1993.

"Following a gain of 14.6 percent in the (International Finance Corp) Composite Index in the first half of 1997, we expect an extension of this strong performance by the emerging markets in the second half of the year," he said.

The International Finance Corp is a unit of the World Bank. The index measures the performances of selected stock markets in such developing markets as East and South Asia, Eastern Europe, Latin America and the Middle East.
Dennis expected the U.S. central bank to raise interest rates 0.25 percent in August, less than the 0.25 to 0.50 percent he had previously expected.
"At worst, any rise in global short-term interest rates may lead to a hiccup in the bull run in the emerging markets and not a major trend correction."

Factors supporting more gains for emerging markets include more countries joining in the rally, the growth of developing nations' economies and corporate earnings and the easing of current account imbalances in Asia.

Risks include a greater-than-expected "deterioration of global liquidity conditions" through much higher U.S. interest rates or Japanese investors selling off U.S. Treasury bonds, and a sharply weaker dollar.
Dennis repeated his recommendation for an overweight position in Latin American markets and underweight in Asia.

"Although Asia is clearly cheap on virtually all absolute historic valuation measures and also cheap relative to Latin America, it is difficult to argue that Latin America is absolutely expensive, a reassuring conclusion for emerging markets as a whole."
